reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: [p. 16-1] Post-construction integrity testing is integral to drilled shaft design and construction. Its most common purpose is quality assurance of concrete placement by measuring a characteristic of the hardened concrete; tests with no permanent effect are 'non-destructive integrity tests' (NDT), and their interpretation and use 'non-destructive evaluation' (NDE). With quality construction and inspection, NDE helps ensure the as-built foundation meets the specifications and will perform as designed, but it must be viewed within a well-designed and executed inspection process, not as a substitute for quality construction or inspection. A second application is evaluating shafts suspected of a defect from construction observations, anomalous cylinder tests or unexpected performance (e.g., excess settlement), to define the problem and decide whether remediation is needed, possibly by destructive methods (coring). Categories: planned tests in the QA procedure (non-destructive, relatively inexpensive, routine on U.S. transportation projects) and unplanned forensic tests (more time-consuming and expensive, needing more extensive evaluation). ASTM D6760 definitions: anomaly - an irregularity or series of irregularities in the NDT results indicating a possible flaw; flaw - any deviation from the planned shape or material characteristics; defect - a flaw that, because of size or location, may significantly detract from the shaft's performance.
key_points: NDT/NDE for QA of concrete placement; not a substitute for quality construction or inspection
Also used to investigate suspected defects (may include coring)
Planned QA tests vs. unplanned forensic tests
ASTM D6760: anomaly (NDT irregularity), flaw (deviation), defect (flaw that may significantly detract)
sections.applicability: Post-construction integrity testing and QA for all drilled shaft projects

sections.title: Non-Destructive Integrity Tests
sections.body: [p. 16-2] The common transportation NDT methods are summarized in Table 16-1. They require expertise: technicians conduct field tests and a qualified engineer, with the project geotechnical engineer, interprets, mostly with specialized software. Agencies should use trained employees or a qualified outside firm; when NDT/NDE is in the construction contract the contractor hires the firm, which can raise questions in disputes over whose interests the firm represents. Table 16-1: CSL (ASTM D 6760): acoustic signals between embedded tubes, velocity and strength evaluate concrete between tubes; concrete inside the cage; difficulty locating defects outside the line of sight, tubes installed with the cage; relatively accurate and low cost, effective in the core; variations cross-hole tomography, perimeter and single hole sonic logging. TIP (ASTM D 7949): temperature from heat of hydration infers geometry, low temperature zones indicate potential defects, cables or tubes embedded; entire cross section; may be less effective at the tip, limited time window; relatively accurate, low cost, fast. Gamma-Gamma (Caltrans Test 233): backscattered gamma counts correlate to density, single probe in access tubes; around the perimeter; detection limited to several inches from tubes just inside the cage, radioactive material management; highly effective around the perimeter.
key_points: Technicians test, a qualified engineer interprets; specialized software
Contractor-hired NDE firms can complicate disputes
Table 16-1: CSL (ASTM D6760, core concrete), TIP (ASTM D7949, whole section), Gamma-Gamma (Caltrans 233, perimeter)
tables: Table 16-1: Common NDT Methods for Drilled Shafts in Transportation Applications - Crosshole Sonic Logging (ASTM D 6760), Thermal Integrity Profiling (ASTM D 7949) and Gamma-Gamma (Caltrans Test 233): basic concept, primary application, limitations, advantages, variations and related tests
sections.applicability: Post-construction QA testing; suspected defect investigation

sections.title: Sonic Methods
sections.body: [pp. 16-3 to 16-9] Crosshole Sonic Logging (CSL), the most widely used QA test (Figure 16-1): water-filled access tubes, typically one per foot of diameter, inside the cage from the base to several feet above cut-off; transmitter and receiver at the same elevation (zero-offset) in two tubes, impulses usually 30 to 50 kHz, logged at increments typically 2 inches while pulled up together; multiple tube pairs locate and size anomalies at low to moderate cost. Results: travel time (First Arrival Time, FAT; V = d/t, d tube spacing) and signal strength (relative energy, RE, in dB); sharp FAT increase with RE decrease indicates potential defects. Theoretical velocity V_c = sqrt(alpha E / rho) (Eq. 16-1), alpha = (1 - nu)/[(1 + nu)(1 - 2 nu)] (Eq. 16-2), rho = gamma / g (Eq. 16-3), g = 32.2 ft/sec^2 (printed as 'G' in the symbol list); for 3,000 to 5,000 psi concrete Eq. 16-1 gives 10,000 to 11,500 ft/second, but normal concrete exhibits about 13,000 ft/sec (frequency effect), sometimes used as a baseline; software usually uses a running average over 10 to 12 ft. Velocity reduction VR = (1 - V/V_b) 100% ~ (1 - V/13,000) 100% (Eq. 16-4); water about 5,000 ft/sec, air about 1,000 ft/sec. Table 16-2 ratings, widely used: VR 0-10%, energy reduction <= 6 dB, Good (G); 10-20%, 6.1 to 9 dB, Questionable (Q); > 20%, > 9 dB, Poor/defect (P/D); no signal (NS), intrusion or severe defect or tube debonding; VR about 60%, >= 12 dB, Water (W). DFI (2018) proposed preliminary FAT-increase guidelines, not recommended to replace Table 16-2 at present. Figure 16-2 (Likens et al., 2007): velocity and energy plot and 'waterfall diagram' (recommended by ASTM D 6760); FAT increases of 40, 38 and 14 percent and energy reductions 7.3, 9.4 and 7.5 dB at 1, 7 and 10.5 m; the 1 m and 7 m anomalies rate Poor/defect in Table 16-2 'and Class C of Table 16-3' (as printed; the printed Table 16-3 is the TIP table). Detectable defect size falls with frequency (theoretically about one-fourth wavelength); Amir and Amir (2009): a defect midway between tubes is detectable only if larger than about one third of the tube spacing or about 10 percent of the section, and defects near a tube appear larger in tomography. Tubes: Schedule 40 steel or PVC, 1.5 to 2-inch inner diameter, inside the cage full length, plugged at the bottom, one per foot of diameter, at least two, vertical and uniformly spaced. PVC suits CSL and gamma-gamma but debonds sooner (test within a few days); steel resists debonding typically at least two weeks but needs calibration for gamma-gamma. Fill tubes with water before concreting (buoyancy, temperature equilibrium); debonding near the top can falsely indicate anomalies, checked by inspecting concrete at cut-off. Test at least all perimeter pairs and main diagonals, all pairs if an anomaly is found. Tubes also serve TIP, gamma-gamma (plastic only), base coring or post-grouting (use drillable plastic bottom caps). Crosshole Tomography (CT): same equipment with vertical offsets and all combinations (Figure 16-3), thousands of ray paths inverted into 2-D or 3-D velocity tomograms (Figure 16-4, Hollema and Olson 2002; Olson 2005); more costly, used when CSL VR exceeds 20 percent (the Figure 16-4 shaft had VR 14 to 26 percent at 36 to 39 ft); a protocol of zero-offset scans plus two offset scans when an anomaly is found avoids remobilization. Perimeter Sonic Logging (PSL): tubes outside the cage (Samtani et al. 2005, Tucson polymer slurry shafts, every anomaly verified), noisier, not widely applied, tubes hard to protect.
key_points: CSL: one water-filled tube per foot of diameter, zero-offset, 30 to 50 kHz, 2-in. increments
V_c = sqrt(alpha E/rho) (Eq. 16-1); alpha (Eq. 16-2); rho = gamma/g (Eq. 16-3); normal concrete about 13,000 ft/s
Detectable defect about 1/3 tube spacing or 10% of section (Amir and Amir, 2009)
PVC debonds within days; steel about two weeks; test perimeter pairs and diagonals, all pairs if anomalous
Crosshole tomography for VR over 20%; perimeter sonic logging an option
equations: Eq. 16-1: V_c = sqrt(alpha E / rho) - theoretical compressional wave velocity in concrete; E modulus of elasticity
Eq. 16-2: alpha = (1 - nu) / [(1 + nu)(1 - 2 nu)] - nu Poisson's ratio
Eq. 16-3: rho = gamma / g - mass density of concrete; gamma unit weight, g = 32.2 ft/sec^2
Eq. 16-4: VR = (1 - V / V_b) 100% ~ (1 - V / 13,000) 100% - CSL velocity reduction; V_b baseline velocity (13,000 ft/sec illustrative)

sections.title: Thermal Method
sections.body: [pp. 16-9 to 16-13] Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP), introduced by Mullins and co-workers (Mullins 2010; Mullins and Winters 2011), is widely accepted under ASTM D7949: monitoring temperature from the heat of hydration over the section and length infers potentially defective concrete, cross-section geometry and cage alignment. Measurements by an infrared probe in access tubes or, most practical, embedded thermal cables on the longitudinal bars (sensors typically every 12 inches, typically one cable per foot of diameter, uniformly spaced; Figure 16-5, with data loggers transmitting hourly). Idealized distribution (Figure 16-6): maximum at the center decreasing radially; top 'roll-off' from convection and radiation and base roll-off from conduction; moving groundwater or river water adds convective loss. Table 16-3: potentially defective concrete from a localized temperature decrease; radius and cover from local versus average temperature with the total concrete volume; cage alignment from diametrically opposite measurements. Potential defects: temperature drops in one or more cables over a depth interval (about 89 ft in Figure 16-7a) indicate lower cement content from mixing with groundwater, soil or drilling fluid. Geometry: the average temperature-radius relation from the concrete volume curve (Chapter 15) converts each reading to radius and cover (Figure 16-7b), lower temperature meaning smaller radius and higher a bulge. Alignment: a decrease on one side with a similar increase opposite means the cage is shifted toward the cooler side, shown by consistent or gradual patterns, not sharp local changes. Advantages: the entire cross section is verified (CSL only the core, gamma-gamma only several inches from tubes) and results are often available within 2 to 3 days. Limitations: measurements only during the elevated temperature window of several days, with no second chance, no long-term strength or post-repair testing; base defects may be masked by the expected base roll-off, so do not rely solely on TIP for the base of wet-method shafts: emphasize base cleanout and tremie inspection and consider an alternative NDT method for the base. TIP is reliable and practical, adding cover and alignment estimates; numerical modeling and signal matching of temperatures (Kranc and Mullins, 2007) is warranted only in special cases.
key_points: TIP (ASTM D7949): heat of hydration measured by cables (one per foot of diameter, sensors every 12 in.) or probes
Table 16-3: local cool zones = potential defects; temperature vs. volume gives radius and cover; opposite cables give cage alignment
Verifies the entire cross section; results in 2 to 3 days
Window of only several days; base defects may be masked by roll-off; do not rely on TIP alone at the base of wet shafts

sections.title: Gamma-Gamma Method
sections.body: [pp. 16-13 to 16-17] Gamma-Gamma Logging (GGL): a single probe with a Cesium-137 source and NaI scintillation detector (Figure 16-8) is retrieved at constant rate in a PVC tube, recording counts per second; for concrete, unit weight is reasonably linear with the natural log of counts. Radius of influence is about half the source-detector spacing: a 10 millicurie source with 6 to 8-inch spacing penetrates about 2 to 3 inches, a 100 millicurie source with 12 to 18-inch spacing about 6 to 8 inches; each probe is calibrated to density; Caltrans requires a radius of detection of 3.0 to 4.5 inches. Caltrans places tubes against the inside of the outermost hoop or spiral with longitudinal bars at 8-1/2 inches circumferential spacing for at least 3 inches clear (about the probe radius), covering the cover zone while avoiding the exterior soil or rock (Figure 16-9). Anomalies: assuming normally distributed density, readings over a consecutive 6-inch interval below the mean minus three standard deviations (probability 1.35 percent, as printed) are anomalous, mean and sigma from all readings excluding anomalous intervals (Figure 16-10, 4-ft cage, four tubes, slurry shaft: base readings not judged severe, a higher zone in two tubes was defective concrete). No ASTM standard; Caltrans 'California Test 233' (2005). Non-density effects: tube-to-steel distance, PVC couplers (typically 20-ft intervals, log their elevations), reinforcement changes, instrumentation, ties, centering wheels in soft soil. GGL is reliable, repeatable, unaffected by vibration, electrical interference or debonding, with no depth limit, and targets the cover zone where caving or poor flow exposes steel to corrosion (Figure 16-11); probes rise at 10 to 15 ft per minute, about 2 hours for a 6-ft, 100-ft shaft (Caltrans, 2010). Limitations: tests about 7 percent of a 6-ft shaft section; may miss defects outside the cage; cannot define lateral extent (CSL better); tubes must be straight and undamaged; ineffective about 1 ft above each tube bottom; blocked tubes; radioactive source requires NRC licensing, certified and monitored personnel and regular recalibration.
key_points: GGL: Cs-137 source and detector in one probe in PVC tubes; ln(counts) about linear with density
Penetration about 2 to 3 in. (10 mCi) to 6 to 8 in. (100 mCi); Caltrans 3.0 to 4.5 in.
Anomaly: consecutive 6-in. readings below mean minus 3 sigma (California Test 233)
Best for the cover zone; tests about 7% of a 6-ft section; ineffective in the bottom foot
Radioactive source: NRC licensing, certified personnel, recalibration

sections.title: Methods Based on Analysis of Stress Waves
sections.body: [pp. 16-17 to 16-22] Sonic Echo (SE) and Impulse Response (IR) (variations: Bending Wave, Parallel Seismic) are not widely used for QA but help when records raise questions and no access tubes exist: a hammer strikes the head and a geophone or accelerometer records reflections from impedance changes (area, wave velocity, density), e.g., the base, soil intrusions or diameter changes; SE is analyzed in the time domain and IR in the frequency domain. SE (Figure 16-12): filtered receiver signals give reflection arrival times, direction and amplitude, and the length from the base reflection and V_c. Impedance decreases ('neck') may be soil intrusion, honeycomb, cold joints or reduced area; increases ('bulb') are generally not defects; non-base reflections are anomalies, classified as potential defects by the engineer with construction observations (caving, underpour). Limitations: echo strength depends on surrounding ground (interpreter needs boring data); echoes too weak beyond L/D of about 10:1 in rock, 20:1 in stiff or hard soils, 40:1 in medium-stiff and 60:1 in very soft soils; weak base echo on clean rock contact; smallest detectable anomaly about 10 percent of the section (Iskander et al., 2001); defect geometry generally undeterminable, though multiple locations on large shafts can locate partial reflections within 3 to 5 diameters of the top; shadowing below a major defect; defects at or near the base indistinguishable; planned diameter changes and truck-to-truck concrete changes appear as anomalies. One-dimensional wave equation matching (Middendorp and Verbeek, 2005) is non-unique. SE is a screening method for defects of at least 10 percent of the section and wrong-depth bases, useful for shafts without access tubes and to confirm CSL or GGL defects. IR: a load-cell hammer; force and velocity transformed by FFT; mobility V/F versus frequency (Figure 16-13): the initial slope reflects low-strain axial stiffness (low compared with sound shafts is anomalous); resonant peaks spaced Delta f = V_c/2L give length, and a reflection at distance Z = V_c/(2 Delta f) (Eq. 16-5); the mobility N, the geometric mean of peaks P and Q, is the inverse of impedance (rho_c V_c A_c), and N greater than calculated is anomalous (reduced area, density or velocity). Finno and Gassman (1998): resolution depends on P/Q (no peaks as it approaches 1.0), governed by L/B and soil-to-concrete velocity and density ratios; the base usually cannot be identified for L/B over 30; casing ends, loose annulus fill, overexcavation and drilling disturbance affect results. Impedance logs (Hertlein and Davis 2006; Gassman and Li 2009) show impedance as equivalent diameter (Figure 16-14, a soil-filled joint).
key_points: SE (time domain) and IR (frequency domain): hammer impact at the head, reflections at impedance changes
For shafts without access tubes, or to confirm CSL or GGL findings
Echo lost beyond L/D about 10 (rock), 20 (stiff soil), 40 (medium-stiff), 60 (very soft); minimum defect about 10% of section
Defects at or near the base and below a major defect generally not identifiable
IR: Delta f = V_c/2L; Z = V_c/(2 Delta f) (Eq. 16-5); base not identifiable for L/B over about 30
equations: Eq. 16-5: Z = V_c / (2 Delta f) - distance from the geophone to a reflection from the impulse response mobility plot; Delta f spacing of resonant peaks, V_c wave velocity in concrete

sections.title: Drilling and Coring
sections.body: [pp. 16-22 to 16-24] Drilling and/or coring is a frequent response to integrity concerns from placement problems or NDT anomalies, giving direct examination and strength tests of as-placed concrete, but it is slow and expensive with limitations. Blind drill competent sections (faster) and core target zones, inferring quality from drilling rate (a drop may reveal a soil-filled cavity). Cores show voids, weak cementation, fractures, soil or slurry intrusions; low recovery may indicate defects. Use double or triple barrel techniques; core diameter ideally four to five times maximum aggregate: NX for 1/2-inch aggregate, 4-inch preferred for 1/4 to 1 inch (as printed). Figure 16-15: (a) continuous core where CSL showed 15 to 20 percent VR, strengths well above the 5 ksi design, no action; (b) quality base contact with rock; (c) poor cementation and bleed channels near the top, chipped and re-poured; (d) weak concrete and poor recovery near the tip after tremie discharge several feet above the base, remediated by hydrodemolition and grouting. Jones and Wu (2005): access and targeting are difficult; rigs need at least 10 ft clear behind the hole and most cannot clear more than 3 ft of projecting steel (raise the ground or use mats or platforms); locate core holes at least 6 inches from steel bars and tubes; several inches of drift is expected, and holes may exit the shaft or hit bars. Coring best characterizes large defects (a collapse leaving no concrete is almost always found); small defects can be missed, and local weak concrete may overstate a defect (e.g., at a rock socket base with good contact elsewhere). Grout or concrete holes after sampling if the shaft will be used.
key_points: Core target zones; blind drill elsewhere and read drilling rate
Double or triple barrel; core diameter 4 to 5 times maximum aggregate
Core holes at least 6 in. from bars and tubes; expect drift (Jones and Wu, 2005)
Best for large defects; small defects missed; fill holes after sampling

sections.applicability: Investigation of suspected defects identified by NDT

sections.title: Downhole Video Inspection
sections.body: [pp. 16-24 to 16-25] Cameras lowered into access tubes or core holes give real-time video at the surface; the camera of Figure 16-16a fits a 2-inch PVC tube or core hole. In Figure 16-16b, a zone of zero core recovery showed continuous concrete with good aggregate distribution, so poor recovery came from the coring equipment or method, not defective concrete.
key_points: Downhole video in access tubes or core holes; can show that poor recovery was a coring artifact

sections.title: Load Testing for Drilled Shaft Integrity Evaluation
sections.body: [p. 16-25] A load test verifies geotechnical and structural resistance only for the test conditions and short duration, so any Chapter 13 method gives some measure of integrity. A rapid load test measures axial or lateral response without prior instrumentation (an unplanned test); high-strain dynamic drop-weight tests at various heights, with strain gauges and accelerometers at the top, can in theory relate stress wave characteristics to strength and stiffness if sufficient resistance is mobilized. A full-scale static axial or lateral test may be warranted for a systematic construction error, one test confirming or rejecting all affected shafts. Not all defects are detectable: insufficient cover may not affect a load test but can affect long-term performance through corrosion. The heading prints 'INTEGITY'.
key_points: Load tests verify integrity only for test conditions and duration
Rapid tests need no prior instrumentation; drop-weight dynamic tests in theory relate waves to strength
Static test can settle a systematic construction error
Cover deficiencies not detected by load tests
sections.applicability: Quality assurance testing for shafts with suspected defects

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: [pp. 16-25 to 16-26] Tests on completed shafts verify concrete integrity, mostly NDT of hardened concrete, each with advantages and limitations, always considered with construction observations. CSL is the most widely used; tomography enhances evaluation; TIP is increasingly used and is the only method assessing the full cross section; gamma-gamma, used extensively by several states, is most effective around the perimeter where cover is critical; coring and load testing investigate suspected defects.
key_points: Interpret NDT with construction observations
CSL most widely used; TIP only full-section method; gamma-gamma for perimeter cover
Coring and load tests for suspected defects
